speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWMs were introduced, championed and coordinated by the Labour Movement, and the nature of them is that they are interventions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: They were introduced in sectors that had either seen market failure in terms of wages or that had wage growth that lagged increases in the costs of living.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is why PWM wage increases are generally higher than National Wage Council recommendations, in order to close the gap of wages in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: But, of course, it is always easy to posit academic questions about what these statistics all really mean.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I wish to offer the perspective of an industry representative who has been part of the process of one of the first PWM sectors and has close interactions with industry representatives from several others.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I declare my interest, Sir, as President of the Security Association Singapore, which represents security companies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I sit on the Security Tripartite Cluster that formulates the PWM for our sector.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: My view is that the PWMs are not just a minimum wage plus scheme.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWM has revalued the work that is done in these sectors, not only in terms of wages, but also in terms of career progression, in terms of perceptions of the jobs in these sectors and their contribution to our economy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: More can be done as the PWMs advance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Most of these low-wage work are in jobs of the hands.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Cleaning, waitering, landscaping, waste management are some of the examples of these jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: With the emphasis on meritocracy in Singapore's development since Independence, jobs of the hands were increasingly seen as unattractive and were relegated to occupations that people would only go into if they were not academically meritorious.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In many cases, these became occupations of last resort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Because the emphasis has been on studying hard to get a good job, it seemed natural that for jobs that did not require academic qualifications, their wages should be low.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In other words, these jobs were valued lowly in terms of how important they were and therefore, how much workers should be remunerated.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: They were also considered low socio-economic status occupations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Hence, wages in the first three PWM sectors – cleaning, security and landscape – had stagnated at a low level for a long time and required intervention.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWMs have already started to challenge how work in these sectors is valued.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: First, because the PWMs stipulate not just wages, but skills and training, the idea that these are generic jobs that anyone could do has been chipped at.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Workers now have to attend courses and pass assessments to be able to qualify for entry into the sector and for promotion to the next rung of the wage ladder.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Essentially, there are now some barriers to entry and advancement.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Second, the PWMs are wage ladders, that recognise increases in skills and experience and essentially create a career path.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It would fall to reason therefore, that workers in the higher rungs of each PWM are performing work that is more valuable, for example supervisory work or work that requires specific skills.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Third, the PWMs prescribe year-on-year wage increases over several years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This means that there is a compounded increase in value over time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Value, of course, does not exist in vacuo.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Value must be ascribed by someone or recognised by someone.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In real terms, value would also suggest that a person is willing to part with something of a certain worth to enjoy the benefits of that item or service.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: So, in what ways has the value of work been enhanced in the PWM sectors and to what extent?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: First, we can look at the value ascribed to these jobs by consumers and society at large.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This suggests that at least for cleaners and security officers, there is significant value placed on the work that they do, such that consumers are willing to pay more for their services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The survey also made reference to the progressive wages in these sectors, so, there was a nexus between the progressive wages and responses in the survey.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, consumers have continued to raise concerns about costs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Cheap-sourcing continues to be the primary method of buying for the outsourced PWM services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Furthermore, while there has been improvement in the treatment of low-wage workers and in their working environments, there are still situations that underscore a continuing discrimination against these workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I had raised in this House in one of my first speeches the absurd situation of a condominium in the Grange area that disallowed security officers and cleaners from using the condominium toilets.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) had instead installed temporary toilets for them at the basement carpark, which did not even have proper lighting nor running water on the weekends.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This was presumably to prevent mixing between residents and workers in the condominium toilets.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: There is therefore still some socio-economic stigma prevailing in some quarters, as regard this type of work and workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Cleaners, for example, have enjoyed an over 70% increase over a decade.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, while of course workers will be happy with mandatory wage increases, have these workers re-considered the value of their own work?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: There are many anecdotal accounts of workers who now put more paid on training and upgrading themselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: A Union of Security Employees study published in 2022 found that over 90% of security officers were prepared to use more technology at work and to undergo training for it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: But, these are not clear indications on whether they feel that the value of their work has appreciated.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: My own experience has been, at least for the security industry, that workers now value their work better and expect to be compensated better.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: By way of background, I joined the security industry the year before the PWM for the sector came into effect, some nine years ago.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: When I first looked at the wages of officers, I was appalled.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: With this significant growth in wages and many having progressed above the basic rung, I have also seen over the years, officers understanding their functions better, taking more pride in what they do and asking for better wages and working conditions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: There is a greater sense of professionalism and more importantly, of dignity.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: And Sir, this is not an academic take on the industry, or a survey, this is what I have seen myself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Pride, Sir, in one's work and dignity in your occupation is something that is truly powerful and it is priceless.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Third, we must look at whether employers in these sectors have re-valued the contributions of their workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In the 2023 Straits Times article, Uniqlo said that "When we have employees who are happy working at Uniqlo (due to the increase in wages), that will translate into excellent customer services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: To a certain extent, that will therefore boost sales".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In another article, cleaning company LS2 Services said, that it recognised their cleaners as "valuable resources contributing to Singapore's clean and green city".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, many employers, especially in the outsourced sectors, still see workers as deployable assets rather than as their company's human capital.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Buyers of outsourced services still complain that some companies are still just deploying manpower rather than providing a skilled service.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: They therefore justify a cheap-sourcing approach because services are indistinguishable – but for the price.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Employers for their part also complain that some workers merely attend at the site to "mark attendance" – but the question is what we need to do to get out of this cycle of finger pointing?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: If a outsourced services company adopts a laissez-faire approach to quality and effectiveness of their manpower, it would invariably lead to a reduction in the perceived value of that occupation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Employers must therefore up their game as well, to offer services that are more cost-effective, more innovative and more productive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWMs moving forward can do so much more.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Looking forward and in the past few years, the Prime Minister has consistently called for a broadening of definitions of success, as well as for remuneration to be based on also on skills and not just academic credentials.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The Prime Minister's vision is one which I support and share, including the Prime Minister's call to fairly remunerate jobs of the hands, which tend to be low-wage work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWMs have, fortuitously, been contributing over the past decade to precisely the Prime Minister 's vision of a labour market where the rewards of work are more fair and equitable.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Looking forward, how can the PWMs continue to contribute to the reshaping of attitudes and perceptions towards low-wage work and consequently, its value?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: First, I think we should acknowledge that it is probably not sustainable nor desirable for the PWMs for all sectors to continue indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: As I set out earlier, PWMs were first conceived to address market failures in wage growth or persistently stagnant wages in specific sectors.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It would appear then, that once these issues are resolved, the PWMs could lose their purpose.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is critical, because otherwise, the PWMs may become a crutch to workers – who will only be able to achieve wage growth due to interventions by the tripartite partners and not through themselves showing the value of their work, nor negotiating for it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In this regard, it is absolutely critical that while the PWMs are in force, we empower workers in these sectors to realise the value of their work, to realise the value of their skills and training and to organically demand for higher wages as they grow in expertise and seniority.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This will position them to be able to continue to grow their value and their wages even if their sector is eased out of the PWM.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: We must avoid this as one of the outcomes of the PWMs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It is also important to note that there are cost consequences of the PWMs beyond just the specific professions covered.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Hence, for example, Starbucks, which is required under the F&B PWM to increase the wages of its baristas, also increased the wages of supervisors and managers to ensure parity and fairness across all job levels.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Each company, after all, will also have to reconcile the PWM job roles and wages with its own internal pay scale and advancement route for all its different types of staff.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: While increases in non-PWM job wages are of course a good thing, the question is sustainability and consequent effect on increases in costs and overall inflation in the economy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I have started to think about what an easing out of the PWMs would entail.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: My view is that it should not mean that the PWM would be removed or no longer apply.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: For sectors that are ready, I would suggest that they should instead evolve into a PWM 2.0 to preserve the wage levels already achieved and to provide a base from which the value of these jobs will continue to be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is important to ensure that wages do not make a u-turn.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: And a possible U-turn is a particular concern in the outsourced sectors, given that the profit of outsourced services companies is based on the difference between the wage of the outsourced worker and the charge out rate by the company.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Second, the skill ladders should remain and should be periodically reviewed, including whether there is a need for further training or refreshers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This will ensure that skills remain relevant and productivity continues to grow.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: One example is how the security industry is looking to train our workers to be AI-literate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Skills and courses like these could be incorporated in the periodic review of the skills ladders to ensure continued growth in the value proposition of workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Third, and perhaps most importantly, the PWMs would not be inactive, they would merely be dormant.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The PWMs in PWM 2.0 will be living, breathing creatures, vigilant and ready to take corrective measures if necessary.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This would include factors like working conditions and workplace safety and health.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In the security industry, we are trying to reduce working hours in a sustainable manner, while adhering to the prescribed PWM wages.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Companies in each sector can also be encouraged to leverage on productivity-building initiatives like the NTUC's company training committees.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In this way, we can continue to enhance the value of low-wage work through the operation of PWM 2.0.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It is unique to Singapore that employers, unions and Government agencies can sit down, negotiate and agree to very wide-ranging increases in wages, year-on-year.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: As Minister Tan said last month, there are many heated debates between tripartite partners behind closed doors, and the periodic PWM negotiations are probably the most heated of them all.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is because the unions make very robust representations and put up a good fight.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: And Sir, I can attest to this, because I am on the opposite side of the table, representing industry, and we come in with equally well-reasoned arguments.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The Government bodies then come in with policy input and objectives, and we negotiate hard to come to a consensus.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Truly, it is something that you cannot fully understand until you are involved in it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: You can be arguing one day, even publicly, and hugging the next.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is because we have a shared objective, to achieve the best for our workers and our businesses.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: We merely differ on occasion, on how to get there.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Our tripartism is precious and we must defend it against unfair criticism and strengthen when needed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I would especially like to thank the team from the NTUC U-Care Centre who are the Secretariat for all the PWM sectoral negotiations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I mention them specifically because theirs is not an easy job.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: They are the ones caught in the middle of these heated discussions, trying to reconcile positions between the tripartite partners and to actually draft the PWMs and statements of the tripartite clusters.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Tripartite partners, including myself, can be very demanding and difficult and sometimes the secretariat itself comes under fire.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: And yet, they trod on, motivated to see through their mission.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In particular, Sir, I would like to express gratitude to Mr Zainal Sapari and Ms Phyllis Lim.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Mr Sapari championed and led the implementation of the earlier PWMs and Ms Lim continues to lead the secretariats.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It is without exaggeration to say that these two people are probably the two people, in Singapore who have contributed the most to the success of the PWMs, and through the PWMs, the uplifting of the lives and livelihoods of tens of thousands of low wage workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: To Mr Sapari and Ms Lim, thank you.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: And I am hopeful, Sir, that one day, we will be able to call “low-wage work” just “work” or even better, “good work”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I also thank the Member for affirming the importance of tripartism to contributing to the success of PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Indeed, our low-wage workers perform essential jobs and should be recognised for their contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They form the backbone of our economy and provide many important services that we should not take for granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And this is why we must ensure that they are paid meaningful wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: A decade ago, tripartite partners recognised that wages in some jobs were stagnating, as Mr Raj Joshua Thomas earlier on shared, especially in outsourced sectors like cleaning, security and landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the same time, workers found themselves entrenched in the same job with little opportunity for skills upgrading and progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In response, NTUC conceptualised the PWM to chart out better wage, skills and career pathways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This gave us confidence and we further expanded PWM to the lift and escalator maintenance sector in 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When I chaired the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers in 2020, I recalled we had several challenges to overcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: First, the lowest paying jobs were in domestic sectors, whether they were in kopitiams, heartland retail, cleaning jobs, security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And this presented the dilemma of how to uplift low-wage workers significantly while convincing consumers and businesses to pay more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The second challenge was raising the coverage of progressive wages from only 10% of low-wage workers in the early days of the first few PWMs and making wage increases meaningful to narrow the gap between the bottom 20% and the median worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To address these challenges, then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong in his National Day Rally speech in 2021 announced the Government's acceptance of the Tripartite Work Group's recommendations to expand PWM to more sectors like food and retail and occupations including administrators and drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And back then, if you recall, we were in the midst of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Despite COVID-19 challenges and business uncertainties, tripartism prevailed and delivered significant boosts in PWM wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The security sector, Mr Raj Joshua Thomas would be very familiar with this, will see even stronger growth, as the Member had highlighted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Today's security PWM wage requirements are minimally at $2,650.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is higher than the P20 salary range today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And that is a 56% increase from 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These significant wage increases are possible for the security sector, in part because of its high potential for productivity gains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Through deployment of digital technologies, more efficient work processes and robust skills certification framework to guide officers in improving their productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But of course, as the Member also shared, we are still working on how to improve their work environment and reduce reliance on work hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Beyond PWM, we also require employers to pay all their local employees at least the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) to qualify for foreign work passes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And we implemented the Progressive Wage Mark Accreditation Scheme to encourage consumers to support employers who are paying progressive wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, as a whole, collectively, these measures benefit up to nine in 10 local full-time low-wage workers today, up from where we were – one in 10 prior to 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we agree with the Member that if we want wages to continue to increase, both workers and businesses must continue to improve productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And this is why the PWM is not just about raising wages, but also raising the value-add of the jobs involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Tripartite partners regularly review the skills letters while workers are required to go through skills training and encouraged to take on higher value jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Businesses too, have a significant role in transforming business models, improving operations, as well as redesigning jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And they can also take reference from the respective industry transformation maps too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we recognise that uplifting low-wage workers is a journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government has thus provided employers substantial transitional support through the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, which partially offsets employers' costs of paying lower-wage workers better wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, employers must take advantage of this transitional support by accelerating business transformation, such as adopting technology and refining processes to improve productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And the security sector has shown that it can be done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Member is right that the success of PWM rests in part on public recognition that PWM jobs are important jobs and that society must support fair remuneration of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When I speak to our low-wage workers across sectors, it is clear that they want their work to be recognised by society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They prefer the dignity of earning a fair salary over receiving handouts any day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And this is fundamental to our social compact here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In this regard, tripartite partners agree with the Member that service buyers and consumers also play important roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This allows service providers to redesign work processes holistically to deliver quality outcomes with lower labour intensity, enabling employers to pay higher wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And it is also important for consumers to treat fellow Singaporeans with respect and recognising that paying a little more for goods and services goes a long way to rewarding their efforts and to improve the livelihoods of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Member spoke on the future of PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I agree that we should regularly take stock and make adjustments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In fact, this is why we had convened the Tripartite Workgroup in 2020, to take stock and to refresh our approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In jobs where the skills levels are higher and wages have risen to an appropriate level, we recognise that their wages could then be decided by market forces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Of course, we hope to see the wages in more jobs rise sufficiently, such that there is no longer a need to mandate PWM wages which increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We will certainly continue to monitor and review PWM together with our tripartite partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It will continue to be a vital pillar of support and uplift for our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Employees must recognise that they have the largest influence on work productivity outcomes in transforming businesses and jobs and supporting the continuous and upskilling of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But at the same time, workers too need to do their part by embracing change and being open to work with technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: If we get this ecosystem right, we will not just uplift our low-wage workers, but also enable our businesses to thrive and our economy to grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And to conclude, I would like to thank our tripartite partners, our employers, our union leaders who have done a lot, and also certainly our members of the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Beyond just paying more, I think what we are doing is to give them respect and dignity for the work that they do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think it is key that we value all our low-wage workers for all they do for us and our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, with that, I want to say a big thank you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Certainly, this is a whole-of-society effort to uplift our low-wage workers for a stronger social compact for Singapore.
